overview.text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is a federal agency whose mission is to protect human health and the environment. President Richard Nixon proposed creating it in Reorganization Plan No. 3 in July 1970 to bring environmental responsibilities that had been spread across government into one agency. December 2, 1970—the day the Senate confirmed EPA’s first administrator, William Ruckelshaus—is traditionally treated as the agency’s birthday. EPA was designed to study pollution across air, water, and land, monitor environmental conditions, and work with states on standards and enforcement. It carries out laws passed by Congress by developing regulations, enforcing them, conducting research, providing grants, and cooperating with state, local, and Tribal governments.

key_facts.text: EPA’s traditional birthday is December 2, 1970, when the Senate confirmed its first administrator; Nixon had signed the reorganization plan calling for the agency in July.
Its mission is to protect human health and the environment, including by supporting clean air, land, and water.
When Congress passes an environmental law, EPA helps implement it by writing regulations; it also enforces regulations and may work with states and Tribes on national standards.
EPA’s creation consolidated environmental responsibilities that had been scattered among parts of the federal government, including responsibilities related to air pollution and water quality.
EPA also studies environmental problems in laboratories and provides grants for work such as scientific studies and community cleanups.
